newsitem.title: UK: UK welfare reform to head Major's election agenda.
newsitem.headline: UK welfare reform to head Major's election agenda.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major planned a fresh attempt to rally his dispirited Conservatives on Saturday by promising the biggest advance in welfare provision for 50 years if they win the election.
With weeks to go until polling day, party sources said Major would also unveil the slogan that the ruling party would campaign under: "You can only be sure with the Conservatives".

But they ruled out the possibility that Major would announce the election date -- widely expected to be May 1 -- when he addresses the annual meeting of the Conservative Central Council in the western England town of Bath.
An election must be held by May 22.
Major's address, due to start at 1100 GMT, comes amid increasing evidence that even his own MPs cannot believe that the Conservatives can win a fifth successive term.
With an opinion poll putting the opposition Labour Party 25 points ahead, two Conservative MPs, both former ministers, on Friday spoke openly about what might follow a defeat for their party.

While Edwina Currie said Major should resign as party leader immediately on losing power, John Biffen raised the prospect of the defeat being so severe that some of the leading candidates to replace him would no longer be MPs.

Their statements drew an apparent rebuke from party chairman Brian Mawhinney, who told the Bath meeting to loud applause: "To every Conservative one message -- if you don't have something to say that will help us win, don't say anything at all."

The sources said Major would claim that recently announced Conservative policy plans for the state to disengage from its role as a provider of pensions and of care homes for the elderly would mean a revolution in welfare.
Conservatives say, for instance, that by saving for pensions with a private insurance company, Britons can win themselves a far more prosperous old age.

The sources said Major would declare that the improvements would be on a scale only seen twice in Britain this century -- once when Liberals introduced old-age pensions in 1910 and then when a Labour government ushered in the welfare state in the late 1940s.
"It is time for the great move forward in public welfare," the sources quoted the prepared text of Major's speech as saying.
"The Conservatism I care about is not just for those who have the self-confidence to make the most of choice," they quoted him as saying.
"It is for everyone -- for those who do not have the best education, do not have a decent home, do not live in a safe neighbourhood."

The sources said the "sure with the Conservatives" campaign slogan was designed to stress that Britons would take a massive gamble in electing a Labour government, few of whose members would ever have been ministers.
They said it was also an implicit criticism of Labour leader Tony Blair for having refused to allow party spokesmen make specific pledges in key policy areas.
